\subsubsection{Statistical characterisation}\label{sss:ctrlamp-mc}

The corner data above gives performance at five process points. It does not give the
fraction of a population that meets a specification, which for four nominally identical
channels is what sets chip yield. This section reports a 200-sample Monte Carlo run of
the same testbench cell, seed 12345, low-discrepancy sampling. All tests run at
\SI{37}{\celsius}, the on-body operating temperature.

Variation type differs by test and is named in every caption. The offset test varies
mismatch only, with the process fixed at typical: its spread is the channel-to-channel
spread within one die. Every other test varies process and mismatch together, giving
die-to-die spread. The two are not comparable and are never combined here.

Gaussian quantities are reported as mean $\pm\,3\sigma$; clipped or skewed ones ---
the margins and the drive currents --- as 1st and 99th percentiles with the worst
sample. Yield is given per channel and, where a specification exists, for the
four-channel chip. Chip yield is approximately $p^4$, so \SI{95}{\percent} of chips
requires \SI{98.7}{\percent} of channels, near \(2.5\sigma\) rather than \(3\sigma\).

Four results follow.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Drive is symmetric but \SI{30}{\percent} short.} Source and sink match to
\SI{6.4}{\percent}, which is the design goal met. Absolute drive averages
\SI{23.0}{\micro\ampere} sourcing and \SI{24.4}{\micro\ampere} sinking against a
\SI{33}{\micro\ampere} target, and 2 of 400 measurements reach it. Because peak current
is the mirror ratio times the tail current, and roughly \SI{1}{\volt} of headroom is
left unused at each rail, the shortfall is closed by raising either term: a mirror ratio
of 6 at the present tail current reaches \SI{33}{\micro\ampere} for
\SI{38.5}{\micro\ampere} of supply.

\item \textbf{Offset is the dominant accuracy term and misses its budget.}
\(\sigma = \SI{4.82}{\milli\volt}\) from mismatch alone, against
\(\sigma \leq \SI{2}{\milli\volt}\). A current-mirror amplifier adds mirror mismatch to
input-pair mismatch, so this is worse than the \SI{3.07}{\milli\volt} of the
folded-cascode design it replaced --- the cost of the symmetry. It appears directly on
the commanded electrode potential and needs trimming or chopping.

\item \textbf{Phase margin is the binding small-signal specification.} Against the
\SI{10}{\pico\farad} test load, 29 of 200 samples fall below the \SI{60}{\degree}
target: \SI{85.5}{\percent} per channel, \SI{53.4}{\percent} across four. No sample is
near instability --- the worst is \SI{59.3}{\degree} --- and the margin is larger into a
real cell, which loads the output node. The target, not stability, is what is missed.

\item \textbf{Regulation error is set by loop gain at the electrode, not by the
amplifier's own gain.} The cell reduces loop gain to \SI{7.9}{\decibel}, a factor of
2.5, so only about \SI{29}{\percent} of the uncorrected error is removed. The result is
\SI{-48}{\milli\volt} of electrode-potential error at \SI{10}{\micro\ampere} of cell
current, against \SI{0.1}{\milli\volt} at zero current. Any accuracy requirement on the
commanded potential under load has to be met by adding gain, not by trimming.
\end{enumerate}

The bias generator is a separate netlist from the amplifier testbench. The two runs
share a seed but not a device set, so their distributions may be compared in aggregate
and not sample by sample.
